# Data Management {#sec-data-management} ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Question :::: ::::{.task-container} - What has been your biggest spreadsheet headache? - Have you ever struggled to understand a spreadsheet because it has: - Inconsistent names - Unclear codings - Notes or annotations without clear meaning :::: ::: [Why we should all be data quality detectives](https://realworlddatascience.net/foundation-frontiers/posts/2025/10/30/data-detectives.html) ## What makes a well organised spreadsheet? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Question :::: ::::{.task-container} What are the issues with this dataset? :::: ::: ### Example - Even though are data is extremely messy, and has a lot of inconsistencies - we can clean and reformat our data with clear code. - My keeping our data cleaning and tidying to the commmand line we ensure that our work is completely reproducible, with a set of documented steps available at all times. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(readxl) data_ranges <- c("A3:F15", "I3:N15", "Q3:V9") # gather each table as a data range lines <- c("A","B","C") # set names for each experiment clean_data <- map2_dfr(data_ranges, lines, ~ read_excel("data/raw/Data.xlsx", # combined all three tables in one tidy dataframe range = .x, na = c("ND", "-"), # choose characters that match NA .name_repair = janitor::make_clean_names) |> # standardise names mutate(line = .y) # add line information to data ) clean_data |> mutate(genotype = str_remove(genotype, "A-")) |> # fix genotype names fill(genotype) # fill in blanks for genotype in line C ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display}
|genotype | tray|sex | larvae| pupae| adults|line | |:--------|----:|:------|------:|-----:|------:|:----| |WT | 6|male | 200| 101| 100|A | |WT | 6|female | 200| 93| 92|A | |WT | 5|male | 200| 108| 108|A | |WT | 5|female | 200| 85| 84|A | |HET | 4|male | 200| 92| 91|A | |HET | 4|female | 200| 95| 95|A |
::: ::: ## Data Organisation Based on [Broman & Woo (2018), Data Organization in Spreadsheets,](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375989?scroll=top&needAccess=true#abstract) Reproducibility in R begins long before you load a file. Poorly structured data silently corrupts analysis, whereas disciplined organization lets you import, wrangle, and model without ad hoc cleaning ### Consistency **Principle**: Every categorical code, variable name, and missing-value marker must be used consistently. Inconsistency leads to type coercion, ambiguous factors, and failed joins. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) data <- tibble( id = 1:5, sex = c("male", "Male", "M", "female", "F"), glucose = c(NA, 5.2, 6.1, 5.7, "") ) data data_clean <- data |> mutate( sex = recode(tolower(sex), "m" = "male", "f" = "female"), glucose = na_if(glucose, "") ) data_clean ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| id|sex |glucose | |--:|:------|:-------| | 1|male |NA | | 2|Male |5.2 | | 3|M |6.1 | | 4|female |5.7 | | 5|F | |
| id|sex |glucose | |--:|:------|:-------| | 1|male |NA | | 2|male |5.2 | | 3|male |6.1 | | 4|female |5.7 | | 5|female |NA |
::: ::: ### Variable and file naming **Principle**: Names are part of your analytical grammar. They must be readable, regular, and machine-safe. See @sec-column-name ### Dates and Times **Principle**: Always store dates in a consistent format e.g. ddmmyyyy See @sec-dates ### One variable per column **Principle**: Each cell holds one atomic value; never embed multiple attributes in one field. See @sec-tidy ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyr) data_messy <- tibble(id = 1:3, combined = c("adult_male", "juvenile_female", "adult_female")) data_messy data_clean <- separate(data_messy, combined, into = c("age_group", "sex"), sep = "_") data_clean ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| id|combined | |--:|:---------------| | 1|adult_male | | 2|juvenile_female | | 3|adult_female |
| id|age_group |sex | |--:|:---------|:------| | 1|adult |male | | 2|juvenile |female | | 3|adult |female |
::: ::: ### Rectangular layout **Principle**: Keep your data rectangular: one header row, variables in columns, observations in rows. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/tidy-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='tidy data overview' width=80%} ::: ::: ### Preserve Raw Data - Never alter the raw data collection files, every time this occurs errors can be introduced and they may not be trackable. ### No Excel formatting as Data Principle: Encoded information via colour blocks or fonts are invisible to R and ambiguous to other users. ### Metadata and Data Dictionaries Principle: Every dataset requires a companion dictionary documenting meaning, units, and type. [Examples of data dictionaries](https://cghlewis.com/blog/data_dictionary/) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ### Validation Checks - Every import should be followed by automated sanity checks see @sec-validate ### File formats and version control - Where possible use plain text (csv/tsv) and version control for transparency ## Summary Disciplined data organization eliminates **ambiguity**, allows **seamless import into R**, and ensures that analysis code represents all transformations transparently. Having a set of company values around data quality and standardisation where data quality is *everyones responsibility* helps prevent errors, and reduce the risk of information being lost when researchers transition across to new roles. **We should all be data detectives!**
